title: Report on Studying at the University of Pennsylvania
paragraphs: From March 2011, for two months, I did my clerkships at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, USA.

CHOP is the No. 1 children's hospital in the US, subdivided into pediatric neurology, hematology, infectious diseases, cardiology, CICU, NICU, PICU and so on, and it was a hospital with well-equipped pediatric facilities. Also, the University of Pennsylvania is a university that takes pride in being an educational university, and all of the doctors were very enthusiastic about teaching.

For my clerkships, I rotated through pediatric hematology in the first month and pediatric cardiology in the second. In the first, pediatric hematology, students basically belonged to the consult team, performed the physical examination and interview of their own patients, and gave presentations based on the information in the chart.

For the presentations, I first presented up to the Assessment/Plan to the fellow, and in the afternoon I presented to the attending. The fellows must have been busy, but they checked my presentations carefully. Also, a female student from the University of Pennsylvania was doing the clerkship at the same time, and she was very good and highly motivated, so she was stimulating. At the end of the clerkship, I gave a case presentation in front of about 30 doctors. It was a very interesting case, so I searched for papers on PubMed and elsewhere and read and summarised several of them. I was nervous, but I learned a great deal.

The second clerkship was in pediatric cardiology, and the curriculum was outpatient in the first week, consult in the second, and ward in the third and fourth weeks. In the outpatient clinic, I did physical examinations together with the doctor while receiving lectures on heart murmurs, pediatric ECGs, cyanosis and so on. Many of the doctors were very enthusiastic about teaching, and some thoroughly taught me until I understood everything. While I wanted to live up to the expectations of the doctors who taught me so eagerly, every day I felt frustrated by my lack of knowledge and understanding. In the consult rotation, as in pediatric hematology, I repeatedly saw patients and presented to the attending. In the ward in the third and fourth weeks, I went to my own patients before the morning rounds and presented them at the rounds every morning. Besides five or six doctors in charge of the ward, two or three nurses and the patients' parents also took part in the morning rounds, so I could never say anything wrong and felt I had to present confidently, which made me very nervous. During the presentations, the attending often gave me assignments, telling me to look something up by the next day. Separately from these, I was given an assignment to choose one heart disease and give a 45-minute presentation on it, from embryology to treatment and what is currently being discussed in papers, so I was desperately busy preparing for it for the last two and a half weeks. This presentation was in a format in which I lectured to the doctors and students while writing on a blackboard, so I had to memorise what I was going to say, and because it lasted 45 minutes, I was very anxious and tense throughout the preparation period. I remember that when I managed to finish the presentation safely and the doctor told me it was excellent, I was so happy I could have jumped for joy.

Outside the clerkships, I had a great time drinking, dancing and going out to eat with students of the University of Pennsylvania and friends in the dormitory. I was surprised when everyone was dancing on the first floor when I returned to the dormitory, but I thought how American it was and joined in. I was also able to attend home parties held by Dr. 西崎, who works at CHOP, and Dr. 兼井, who works in NY. Being able to hear directly from Japanese doctors working in the US was a very valuable experience.

I am very grateful to have been given such a valuable experience as a medical student. I think everything I felt and learned from this experience will be a treasure in my life. I would like to take this opportunity to sincerely thank everyone at the International Exchange Office, the professors of Nagoya University, the professors of the University of Pennsylvania, the seniors who told me all kinds of information, my classmates who studied abroad with me and supported me mentally, and my parents. Thank you very much.
